Week 3 · Skill Lab

Vocabulary in Context

Work out unfamiliar, technical, and multi-meaning words from the sentences around them — and read figurative language for what it actually means.

By the end of this lab you will be able to

  • ✓Use four kinds of context clue to define an unfamiliar word
  • ✓Break a long word into prefix, root, and suffix to estimate its meaning
  • ✓Choose the right meaning of a multi-meaning word for the sentence in front of you
  • ✓Identify and interpret metaphor, simile, idiom, personification, and hyperbole

Course outcomes covered

  • Determine the meaning of unfamiliar, technical, or multi-meaning words using context clues and word roots
  • Interpret figurative language, including metaphors, similes, and idioms, in context

From the ENG0300 course syllabus.

1Learn

How this skill works

Read this first. Everything after it assumes these ideas.

Four context clues that do most of the work

On a reading test you are almost never expected to already know a hard word. You are expected to work it out from its neighbors. Four patterns cover most cases.

Clue typeWhat to look forExample
DefinitionThe meaning is given outright, often after a comma, a dash, or "which means."Her deductible — the amount she pays before coverage begins — was $1,500.
ExampleInstances follow, often after "such as," "including," or "for example."Perishable goods, such as milk, produce, and fresh fish, must be refrigerated.
ContrastAn opposite is offered, signaled by "but," "unlike," "however," or "instead."The first draft was verbose, but the final version was tight and plain.
InferenceNo direct clue; the surrounding situation narrows the meaning.After three refusals, her tone grew more strident, and the clerk finally called a manager.

Test tip

Read the sentence with a blank where the hard word is, decide what word you would put there, then look at the choices. Predicting first keeps a familiar-looking wrong answer from pulling you off.

Word parts get you close enough

When context is thin, take the word apart. A prefix goes before the root and changes its meaning; a suffix goes after and usually changes the word's job in the sentence.

  • You do not need the exact dictionary definition — close enough usually eliminates three choices.
  • Combine both tools: use word parts to estimate, then use context to confirm.
PartMeaningExample
un-, in-, non-notunfinished, inaccurate, nonrefundable
pre-, fore-beforepreapproval, foresee
re-again, backreapply, reimburse
-able, -ibleable to betransferable, eligible
-tion, -mentthe act or result ofcertification, enrollment
-lesswithoutpaperless, careless

Multi-meaning words are decided by the sentence

Common words carry several meanings, and TABE items often test the meaning you use least. Charge can mean a fee, an accusation, an electrical property, or a rush forward. Run can mean to jog, to operate, or to campaign.

The question is never what the word usually means. It is what the word means here. Substitute your candidate meaning back into the sentence and check that it still reads correctly.

Figurative language says one thing to mean another

  • First ask what the phrase would mean literally, then ask what the author is actually claiming.
  • A figurative-language item usually has one literal-minded distractor. It restates the image instead of interpreting it.
TypeHow it worksExample
SimileCompares using like or as.The training manual was as dense as a tax form.
MetaphorStates the comparison directly, without like or as.Her second job was a treadmill she could not step off.
IdiomA fixed phrase whose meaning is not literal.The proposal was dead in the water.
PersonificationGives human qualities to something not human.The old furnace groaned all winter.
HyperboleDeliberate exaggeration for effect.The line at the DMV took a lifetime.
2See It

A worked example

Watch the reasoning before you try it. Notice the order of the moves — that order is the skill.

Defining a technical word from its context

Open Enrollment

Health175 words

Every fall, employees are asked to choose a health plan during a short window called open enrollment. The choice is harder than it looks, because the plan with the lowest monthly premium is not always the cheapest plan overall.

A premium is what you pay each month simply to have coverage, whether or not you see a doctor. A deductible is different: it is the amount you must pay yourself before the plan begins paying its share. A plan with a low premium often carries a high deductible, which means low monthly cost but a large bill the first time you need care.

Employees who rarely see a doctor may come out ahead with the low-premium plan. Employees managing an ongoing condition usually do not, because they will reach that deductible early in the year and keep paying full price until they do.

Original passage — BEOC Academic Bridge

The question

As used in the passage, what does deductible mean?

Thinking it through

  1. 1

    Find the word and read the sentence containing it.

    "A deductible is different: it is the amount you must pay yourself before the plan begins paying its share."

  2. 2

    Identify the clue type.

    This is a definition clue. The meaning is stated outright right after the colon. That is the fastest kind to use.

  3. 3

    Confirm with the surrounding contrast.

    The passage sets deductible against premium — monthly cost versus what you pay before coverage kicks in. The contrast confirms the definition rather than competing with it.

  4. 4

    Check the definition against the last paragraph.

    Someone with an ongoing condition reaches the deductible early and pays full price until then. That only makes sense with the definition I have, so it holds.

The answer

The amount a person must pay out of pocket for care before the health plan starts paying its share.

Take this with you

When a definition clue is present, the answer is usually within one sentence of the word. Look there before reasoning from scratch.

Reading the Lease

Informational68 words

The lease looked standard until the eleventh page, where a clause stated that the tenant would forfeit the security deposit if the apartment was vacated before the term ended. Marisol had planned to move for a job in the spring. Unlike the flexible month-to-month arrangement she had before, this agreement gave her no way to leave early without losing the deposit entirely.

4Practice

Practice on a full passage

A longer passage with several questions. Check each answer as you go.

The Grid in August

Science235 words

1On the hottest afternoons of the summer, the regional power grid strains under a load it was never designed to carry all at once. Utilities call these hours peak demand — the narrow window, usually between four and seven in the evening, when air conditioners, ovens, and returning commuters all draw power simultaneously.

2To keep the system stable, utilities can ask large customers to curtail usage, reducing their draw voluntarily in exchange for a lower rate the rest of the year. Factories dim lights. Warehouses shift equipment runs to the night. A hospital cannot participate, but a bottling plant often can.

3When voluntary reductions are not enough, the utility may lower voltage slightly across a region. Older residents still call this a brownout, because decades ago it made incandescent bulbs visibly dim. Modern lighting rarely shows it, so most customers now feel nothing at all.

4Grid operators describe August as walking a tightrope in the wind. The comparison is deliberate. The margin between supply and demand on those afternoons is thin, and the consequences of losing balance are immediate and public.

Original passage — BEOC Academic Bridge

6Answer Review

Why each answer is right or wrong

The reasoning behind every choice, including the ones designed to catch you.

Work through the practice first, then open a question below to see the full reasoning. Reading why a wrong answer is wrong is what stops you from choosing it again on the test.

Practice set

Q1As used in paragraph 2, curtail most nearly means —▾

Correct answer: A. to cut back

Why: The sentence defines it immediately: curtail usage, "reducing their draw voluntarily." The examples that follow — dimmed lights, shifted equipment runs — confirm it.

Every choice, explained

  • A.to cut back — Correct. The passage restates curtail as reducing, and every example is a reduction.
  • B.to measure — Measurement never appears. The utility is asking for a change in behavior, not a reading.
  • C.to pay for — Payment moves the other direction in this passage: customers get a lower rate for participating.
  • D.to restore — The opposite of the context. Restoring usage would worsen the problem being described.
Q2In paragraph 1, the word load refers to —▾

Correct answer: B. the total demand for electricity the system must supply

Why: Load is a multi-meaning word. Here it is defined by what follows: air conditioners, ovens, and commuters all drawing power at once. That is electrical demand.

Every choice, explained

  • A.a quantity of goods being transported — A common meaning of load, but nothing in this passage is being transported.
  • B.the total demand for electricity the system must supply — Correct. Paragraph 1 spells out what makes up the load — simultaneous electricity use.
  • C.a burden of responsibility carried by utility workers — A figurative meaning the passage does not use. The strain described is on the grid, not on workers.
  • D.the weight of equipment on transmission towers — Physical weight is a real meaning of load but is unrelated to peak demand hours.
Q3In paragraph 4, the phrase walking a tightrope in the wind is an example of which type of figurative language, and what does it mean?▾

Correct answer: C. Metaphor; managing the grid in August requires fine balance under conditions that could upset it at any moment.

Why: The comparison is stated directly, with no like or as, which makes it a metaphor. The final sentence interprets it for you: a thin margin, with immediate consequences if balance is lost.

Every choice, explained

  • A.Personification; the grid is described as if it were a person. — No human qualities are given to the grid; the image describes the operators' task.
  • B.Hyperbole; the author exaggerates to argue that the grid will fail. — The author is not exaggerating — the last sentence treats the risk as real and specific.
  • C.Metaphor; managing the grid in August requires fine balance under conditions that could upset it at any moment. — Correct. A direct comparison, and the passage explains exactly what it stands for.
  • D.Idiom; it is a fixed expression meaning to work slowly and carefully. — It is a vivid comparison built for this passage, not a fixed everyday expression.
Q4Which context clue best explains the meaning of brownout in paragraph 3?▾

Correct answer: C. A definition clue explaining that voltage is lowered slightly and once made bulbs visibly dim

Why: The paragraph gives the cause (voltage lowered slightly) and the historical effect (incandescent bulbs dimming) in the same breath. That is a definition clue.

Every choice, explained

  • A.A contrast clue comparing it to a blackout — Blackout never appears in the passage.
  • B.An example clue listing appliances that stop working — No appliances are listed in paragraph 3, and nothing stops working.
  • C.A definition clue explaining that voltage is lowered slightly and once made bulbs visibly dim — Correct. The meaning is stated directly around the word.
  • D.An inference clue based on the word brown — Guessing from the color would not produce the meaning. The passage supplies it instead.
